summary: Describes the APEX access service, found at the well-known endpoint named apex=access. It controls who may use the APEX relaying mesh and other APEX services. The protocol is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3341 describes the access service of APEX, a messaging system where relays pass messages between addresses inside one organisation. The service holds a list of permissions, each one saying who may do what to whom, and offers three ways to use that list: ask whether an action is allowed, read an entry, or change one.

questions: what is the apex access service
can you use wildcards in access entries
how does a relay check permissions
subtitle: The service that decides who may send what to whom across an APEX relaying mesh.

tldr.problem: An APEX administrative domain runs a mesh of relays that can pass messages to any endpoint in the domain, so something has to decide which addresses may use that mesh and which services each one may reach.
tldr.mechanism: The access service keeps access entries, each naming an owner, an actor, a list of permitted actions and a timestamp. An application can ask whether an action is allowed, fetch an entry, or replace one, and the service also notifies the owner whenever an entry changes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the entry format, the wildcard matching rules, the three operations and the XML syntax they use. It is Historic today, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it.

today: RFC 3341 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in July 2002 as a Standards Track protocol defining the access service of the APEX relaying mesh.

sections.title: What the APEX Access Service Does
sections.content:
The APEX access service is built on top of the APEX relaying mesh and is used to control use of that mesh and of the other APEX services. APEX, at its core, provides a best-effort datagram service. Within an administrative domain, every relay must be able to handle messages for any endpoint in that domain.

APEX services are logically defined as endpoints, but because they have ubiquitous semantics they do not need to sit on a single physical endpoint. They may instead be provisioned alongside each relay in the domain, even though they are logically provided on top of the relaying mesh. Applications reach a service by exchanging data with a well-known endpoint. The access service lives at the well-known endpoint apex=access, so apex=access@example.com is the access service in the example.com administrative domain.

The access service is not only there for applications. Within a single administrative domain the relaying mesh itself consults it, to decide whether an originator is allowed to transmit data to a recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: APEX relays can carry a message to any address inside the organisation, so something has to check who is allowed to send to whom. That something is the access service, which every relay in the domain can ask.

sections.title: Access Entries and Wildcards
sections.content:
Each administrative domain maintains one or more access entries for each of its endpoints and associated subaddresses, whether or not those addresses are currently attached to the relaying mesh. A separate entry is needed for every actor or group of actors whose permissions are specified. Each entry has four attributes and no content: owner, the address the entry is about; actor, the address granted permission; actions, the permissions granted; and lastUpdate, when the service last created or changed the entry.

An action is a service and operation pair, so presence:publish means the publish operation of the presence service. Two service names are reserved: all, meaning every service, and core, meaning the service implemented by the relaying mesh itself, so that the core:data permission is the one the mesh consults. Two operation names are reserved: all, meaning every operation, and none, meaning no operation at all, written all:none.

The actor is an APEX address, and both its local part and its domain part may carry limited wildcards. The local part may be a literal name such as fred, a subaddress wildcard such as fred/* or apex=pubsub/*, the value apex=* meaning all APEX services, or a lone asterisk meaning any address other than an APEX service. The domain part may be a fully qualified name, a domain wildcard such as *.example.com, or a lone asterisk meaning all administrative domains. A domain wildcard matches zero or more subdomains, so *.example.com matches example.com itself as well as foo.example.com and bar.foo.example.com.

Four default entries are provided for each owner, and an explicitly supplied entry with the same actor value overrides the matching default:

  • local@domain gets all:all, that is, every operation of every service;
  • apex=*@domain gets all:all;
  • apex=*@* gets core:data;
  • *@* gets all:none.

So an explicit entry giving *@* the actions core:data lets endpoints in any domain send data to the owner through the relaying mesh, without disturbing the default that gives the owner's own domain full access. APEX endpoint names may legitimately contain an asterisk, so access entries use a backslash followed by an asterisk to mean a literal one, and two backslashes for a literal backslash. That convention applies to the actor attribute of the get operation and of the access entry in a set operation, but not to the query operation, which allows no wildcards at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Each permission record names one address (the owner), one address or pattern (the actor), and what the actor may do to the owner. Patterns let one record cover a whole group, such as everyone in a domain. A record that names one person beats a pattern, and a pattern that is more specific beats a broader one.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Access Entry
sections.content:
Because actors may carry wildcards, several access entries can apply to a given owner and actor. The RFC gives the algorithm for choosing between them. First, consider only the entries associated with the given owner. Then consider only those entries whose actor value matches the actor address in the query, where a wildcard character can be replaced only by a non-empty sequence of characters to make the match.

The remaining entries are ordered with two keys. The primary key is how exact the match is on the domain part of the actor value, and the secondary key is how exact the match is on the local part. On the domain side an exact match is best, and otherwise the shorter the wildcard match the higher the priority, so for an actor whose domain is bar.foo.example.com a match against *.foo.example.com is better than one against *.example.com. The local part works the same way, whether the wildcard is a subaddress or a service, with one extra note: a local part with a wildcard subaddress does not match the same local part without one.

The RFC works this through with a set of entries for the owner fred@example.com. An entry naming wilma@example.com with all operations covers wilma and the APEX services of the domain for every operation. An entry naming mr.slate@example.com with core:data lets mr.slate send data through the mesh but nothing else. An entry whose owner is the subaddress fred/appl=wb and whose actor is barney/appl=wb lets that actor send data to that subaddress only. An entry for *@example.com with core:data, presence:subscribe and presence:watch gives the rest of the domain those three permissions. An entry for *@* with core:data gives any address outside the domain the right to send data, whether or not it is an APEX service. Although the four default entries are always available, an explicit entry for *@* overrides the matching default.
sections.plainLanguage: When more than one record could apply, the service picks the tightest one. An exact address beats a pattern, and among patterns the shorter one wins, so a rule for one subdomain is preferred over a rule for the whole domain.

sections.title: The Three Operations
sections.content:
A consumer of the service starts by sending data containing a query, get or set operation, and the service replies. When an access entry changes, the service sends a notification to the owner. An implementation must keep access entries in persistent storage.

The query operation asks whether one or more actions are allowed. It carries an owner, an actor without wildcards, a list of actions and a transaction identifier, and it has no content. The service treats the owner as the subject and then: sends a reply with code 553 if the subject is outside this administrative domain; sends a reply with code 550 if the subject is not a valid address; sends a reply with code 537 if the subject's entry matching the originator does not contain an access:query token; selects the entry matching the actor as described above; then sends an allow element if all the permissions in the query are contained in the selected entry, and a deny element otherwise. The transaction identifier in the reply is always the one from the query.

The get operation retrieves the entry for an owner and actor, usually so that it can be updated afterwards, because a successful get returns the lastUpdate value that a later set needs. It carries an owner, an actor, which may contain wildcards, and a transaction identifier. The service again answers 553, 550 or 537, the last now for an access:get token, then selects the entry whose actor attribute matches the requested actor exactly. If there is no such entry it replies with code 551, and otherwise it returns a set element carrying that entry.

The set operation creates, replaces or deletes an entry. It carries a transaction identifier and an access element, which has an owner, an actor, an optional actions attribute and an optional lastUpdate attribute. The actions attribute is present only when adding or replacing an entry, and the lastUpdate attribute only when replacing or deleting one, in which case it gives the current timestamp of the entry to be replaced. The service answers 553, 550 or 537, the last now for an access:set token, and selects the entry whose actor matches exactly. If no entry exists but a lastUpdate was supplied, it replies with code 555. If no entry exists and no lastUpdate was supplied, it creates the entry, sets its lastUpdate to the service's own current date and time, replies with code 250 and sends a set element for the new entry to the subject. If the entry exists but its lastUpdate differs from the one supplied, it replies 555. If the supplied access element has no actions attribute, the entry is deleted, a reply with code 250 is sent, and a set element without actions goes to the subject. Otherwise the entry is updated, its lastUpdate is set to the service's current date and time, a reply with code 250 is sent, and a set element for the updated entry goes to the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three things a client can do. It can ask a yes or no question about a permission, read back a permission record, or write a new one. Reading and writing use the exact actor name as a key, so wildcards only matter when asking the question.

sections.title: How the Messages Are Carried
sections.content:
The operations are XML elements, carried as MIME content exchanged as a BEEP payload. The RFC shows two ways to do this. The first uses a multipart/related message whose parts have the type application/beep+xml, with the outer data element referring to the second part by a content identifier. The second puts everything in a single application/beep+xml message, with the data element carrying a data-content element named Content that holds the operation. The RFC also prints the document type definition for the service, which declares the query, get, set, allow and deny elements with their attributes, and the access element with its owner, actor, optional actions and optional lastUpdate attributes.

One point about deleting needs care. Because access control supports limited wildcarding of actors, deleting the entry for a particular owner and actor combination may modify permission rather than remove it. The RFC therefore uses the special action all:none for that case: an entry for barney@example.com listing core:data, presence:subscribe and presence:watch is not replaced by a deletion, because the separate entry for *@example.com would still grant some of those permissions. Setting that entry's actions to all:none is the way to express the intent to remove them.

The RFC is also explicit that the get and set operations perform no special wildcard processing. An actor value in an access entry may contain wildcard characters, but those have special significance only when a query is performed; for retrieval and update the actor values are treated simply as literal names.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are XML written in the usual markup style, carried inside MIME containers over BEEP. The RFC also gives the grammar, so two implementations know the same element names mean the same thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC refers the reader to the APEX core document for a discussion of security issues, and adds one point of its own. Timestamps issued by the access service may disclose location information, because a timestamp carries a time zone offset. If that information is considered sensitive, the special timezone value -00:00 may be used, after converting the local time accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: The service stamps each permission record with the time it last changed. That stamp includes a time zone offset, which can reveal roughly where the service is, so the RFC offers a way to blank that out.

viz.caption: THE FOUR DEFAULT ENTRIES PROVIDED FOR EACH OWNER
A QUERY AND ITS ALLOW REPLY AS THE RFC PRINTS THEM

data.title: Query and allow
data.code:
<data content='#Content'>
  <originator identity='fred@example.com' />
  <recipient identity='apex=access@example.com' />
  <data-content Name='Content'>
    <query owner='fred@example.com' transID='1'
           actor='barney@example.com'
           actions='core:data presence:subscribe' />
  </data-content>
</data>

<data content='#Content'>
  <originator identity='apex=access@example.com' />
  <recipient identity='fred@example.com' />
  <data-content Name='Content'>
    <allow transID='1' />
  </data-content>
</data>

viz.caption: THE REPLY CODES THE ACCESS SERVICE RETURNS

items.label: Success
items.desc: The entry was created, updated or deleted.

items.label: Permission denied
items.desc: The originator's own entry lacks the access:query, access:get or access:set token.

items.label: Invalid address
items.desc: The subject does not refer to a valid address.

items.label: Entry not found
items.desc: A get found no access entry with that exact actor value.

items.label: Outside the domain
items.desc: The subject is outside this administrative domain.

items.label: Timestamp mismatch
items.desc: The supplied lastUpdate does not match the stored entry, or an entry was to be replaced but none exists.
